output_json.patch_notes: Root cause fix: StringLookupFactory.addDefaultStringLookups(Map<String, StringLookup>) is the sole method that populates the lookup map used by every opt-out/default interpolator entry point (interpolatorStringLookup(), StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator(), and InterpolatorStringLookup(stringLookupMap, defaultStringLookup, addDefaultLookups=true)). Added a private EnumSet<DefaultStringLookup> UNSAFE_DEFAULT_LOOKUPS = {SCRIPT, DNS, URL} and skip those entries in the values() loop unless the new public constant DEFAULT_STRING_LOOKUPS_PROPERTY system property is set to "true" (checked via Boolean.getBoolean at call time, so it is re-evaluated on every non-singleton call). The "base64" alias line and all other ~13 safe default lookups (base64Decoder/Encoder, const, date, env, file, java, localhost, properties, resourceBundle, sys, urlDecoder, urlEncoder, xml) are unaffected. StringLookupFactory.scriptStringLookup()/dnsStringLookup()/urlStringLookup() and the underlying singletons (ScriptStringLookup.INSTANCE etc.) are untouched — direct, explicit use remains possible and documented as an intentional opt-in, per the alert's own guidance (bypass item 4). Updated three existing tests that asserted the old (vulnerable) default behavior: StringLookupFactoryTest (added assertUnsafeKeysExcludedByDefault + a new opt-in test using the system property), and StringSubstitutorWithInterpolatorStringLookupTest (testJavaScript/testDnsLookup* now assert the ${script:...}/${dns:...} tokens are left unresolved by the default interpolator, plus new explicit-opt-in tests calling the lookups directly). Full existing suite (1219 tests) still passes; the provided PoV now prints "NOT VULNERABLE" and exits 1 after the fix (was "VULNERABLE"/exit 0 before).
output_json.risk_notes: This is a documented, intentional behavior change to a public API default (matches the real-world upstream commons-text CVE-2022-42889 fix pattern): StringLookupFactory.INSTANCE.interpolatorStringLookup(), StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator(), and any caller passing addDefaultLookups=true will no longer resolve ${script:...}, ${dns:...}, or ${url:...} tokens by default — those tokens are now left as literal unresolved placeholders (or trigger the configured undefined-variable behavior) instead of executing. Applications that legitimately depended on the old default-on behavior can restore it globally via the new -Dorg.apache.commons.text.StringSubstitutor.enableInterpolationLookup=true system property, or per-call by adding StringLookupFactory.INSTANCE.scriptStringLookup()/dnsStringLookup()/urlStringLookup() to a custom lookup map — both paths are covered by tests. No other lookups, no ScriptStringLookup/DnsStringLookup/UrlStringLookup internal logic, and no StringSubstitutor core substitution logic were touched, keeping the change narrowly scoped to the trust boundary (the default lookup registration).
output_json.summary: Fixed CWE-094 (Text4Shell / CVE-2022-42889-class) code injection: StringLookupFactory.addDefaultStringLookups(Map) — the single shared method that populates every "default"/opt-out interpolator entry point (StringLookupFactory.INSTANCE.interpolatorStringLookup(), StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator(), and any InterpolatorStringLookup constructed with addDefaultLookups=true) — no longer registers the "script", "dns", or "url" lookups by default. These three lookups are the ones capable of arbitrary code execution (ScriptStringLookup -> ScriptEngine.eval, reaching Runtime.exec via Java interop) or SSRF/DoS (DnsStringLookup, UrlStringLookup) when resolved against attacker-influenced template text — exactly the sink all four alert traces converge on. A new opt-in system property, StringLookupFactory.DEFAULT_STRING_LOOKUPS_PROPERTY ("org.apache.commons.text.StringSubstitutor.enableInterpolationLookup"), restores the old default-inclusive behavior for callers who deliberately want it; explicit, intentional use remains available unconditionally via StringLookupFactory.INSTANCE.scriptStringLookup()/dnsStringLookup()/urlStringLookup() and via ScriptStringLookup.INSTANCE directly (documented, non-default APIs, matching upstream's own guidance that direct/explicit use is an intentional opt-in, not a defaultable trust boundary). Because the guard sits at the single map-population choke point (addDefaultStringLookups), it uniformly blocks all 4 alert traces (they all differ only in which StringSubstitutor.replace(...) overload builds the source buffer before funneling into the same substitute()/resolveVariable() -> InterpolatorStringLookup.lookup() -> ScriptStringLookup.lookup() path), and also blocks same-class bypass variants: case/whitespace variants of the prefix (InterpolatorStringLookup.toKey() lower-cases before the map lookup, and the key is simply absent now), any script-engine name behind the "script:" prefix, nested/recursive interpolation that tries to re-introduce "${script:...}" via another enabled lookup (env/sys/properties), and the sibling "dns"/"url" SSRF-class lookups (fixed in the same change, not left for a follow-up).
